output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation demonstrates a posterior-predominant cortical profile. Visuospatial and visuoconstructive abilities are severely impaired: Judgment of Line Orientation 12/30, Hooper Visual Organization 11/30, Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure Copy 8/36 (delayed recall 4/36, limited by the copy). Trail Making A 95 s and B 210 s are markedly slowed, with visual search demands contributing; digit span forward and backward are within normal limits. Verbal learning is below expectation (CVLT-II total 44/80; long delay free recall 9/16) with recognition within normal limits (15/16), a retrieval rather than a storage pattern. Confrontation naming is mildly impaired (Boston Naming Test 52/60); letter and category fluency are within normal limits. Screening: MMSE 24/30, MoCA 17/30. Profile is most consistent with a posterior cortical syndrome, at a level consistent with mild dementia given the reported functional decline.

findings.signal: cortical_retention: Elevated cortical-to-cerebellar SUVr of 1.62 (positive threshold >1.11); distribution: Diffuse cortical retention involving bilateral frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital cortices, highest in the posterior cingulate, precuneus and lateral parietal cortex; loss of grey-white contrast in multiple cortical regions

output.impression: POSITIVE amyloid PET: moderate-to-frequent neuritic plaque density. Cortical SUVr 1.62, above the positivity threshold of 1.11.

output.impression: FDG-PET demonstrates marked bilateral parieto-occipital and posterior cingulate hypometabolism with relative preservation of frontal, medial temporal, and subcortical metabolic activity

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MMSE 24/30 with Balint features, alexia, Gerstmann features and apraxia; recall helped by cues; husband confirms 8 months of decline in reading, face recognition, navigation and dressing; instrumental independence lost (driving, walking out alone, appointments): mild dementia
action_criteria.label: Perform a structured cognitive and behavioural assessment with informant history: a validated bedside instrument with the per-domain breakdown, whether delayed recall improves with cueing, and an explicit account of which instrumental activities have been lost. The syndrome must be documented before it is attributed
action_criteria.rationale: A patient referred by her ophthalmologist for reading difficulty needs the higher-order visual and parietal signs documented and staged by function before they are attributed [PCA_consensus_2017].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Severe visuospatial and visuoperceptual impairment (Judgment of Line Orientation 12/30, Hooper 11/30, Rey copy 8/36) with relatively preserved verbal memory (normal recognition), attention and fluency: a posterior cortical syndrome
action_criteria.label: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile and establish a baseline for tracking
action_criteria.rationale: Normed testing shows a visuospatial-predominant profile with relatively spared memory, which defines posterior cortical atrophy and gives a baseline [PCA_consensus_2017].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TSH, B12, folate, homocysteine, RPR, HIV, renal, hepatic and inflammatory markers normal: no reversible cause
action_criteria.label: Order the cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
action_criteria.rationale: Treatable contributors must be excluded before a neurodegenerative cause is accepted [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Posterior-predominant parieto-occipital, posterior cingulate and precuneus atrophy (left more than right) with relative sparing of medial temporal structures; Fazekas grade 2; no restricted diffusion
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with dementia (volumetric) protocol to define the atrophy pattern and exclude stroke, mass, prion-type diffusion change and vascular disease
action_criteria.rationale: MRI excludes a structural lesion and prion-type diffusion change and shows the posterior atrophy that supports a neurodegenerative cause [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amyloid positivity: decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio with raised p-tau181 and total tau, or a positive florbetapir PET (SUVr 1.62)
action_criteria.label: Establish amyloid status with CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET when the result would change management
action_criteria.rationale: Either CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau or amyloid PET establishes amyloid status; one conclusive test is enough, and it is needed when the diagnosis remains uncertain after the clinical, neuropsychological and MRI assessment or when disease-modifying treatment is being considered [NIA_AA_2018] [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral temporoparietal, occipital, posterior cingulate and precuneus hypometabolism (left more than right) with frontal and medial temporal sparing
action_criteria.label: Consider FDG-PET if the syndrome or its cause remains uncertain after clinical assessment, labs and MRI
action_criteria.rationale: A parieto-occipital metabolic pattern supports posterior cortical atrophy and separates it from corticobasal and Lewy body patterns [Foster_2007].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in APP, PSEN1 or PSEN2
action_criteria.label: Offer an early-onset Alzheimer gene panel after pre-test genetic counselling; do not use APOE genotype as a diagnostic test
action_criteria.rationale: Onset at about 61 makes this early-onset Alzheimer disease, so a counselled APP/PSEN1/PSEN2 panel may be offered, although dementia in her mother at 78 and an aunt in her late 60s does not suggest a dominant variant [ACMG_NSGC_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Additive QT prolongation risk with escitalopram 10 mg: baseline ECG and electrolytes before donepezil; no relevant interaction with lisinopril or acetaminophen; baseline heart rate 72 bpm
action_criteria.label: Check donepezil against escitalopram and her other medicines before starting a cholinesterase inhibitor
action_criteria.rationale: She takes escitalopram, which with donepezil adds QT prolongation risk, so the combination must be reviewed before treatment is offered [NICE_NG97].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal sinus rhythm, rate 70, QTc 424 ms: no conduction or QT contraindication to donepezil
action_criteria.label: Obtain a baseline ECG before starting donepezil alongside escitalopram
action_criteria.rationale: Donepezil and escitalopram both prolong the QT interval and donepezil slows conduction, so a baseline tracing is reasonable before treatment [NICE_NG97].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the reading and visual complaints to an ocular cause or to her anxiety disorder without completing the cognitive work-up
Do not add a benzodiazepine for the worsening anxiety; it impairs cognition and raises falls risk in a patient with visuospatial dementia
Do not start memantine at the mild dementia stage; it is indicated for moderate or severe Alzheimer disease [NICE_NG97]
required_recommendations: Obtain collateral history from her husband about onset, course and daily function

Offer a trial of a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine) for mild Alzheimer dementia after checking pulse, conduction history and current medicines, and a baseline ECG because of escitalopram [NICE_NG97].

Offer amyloid biomarker testing (CSF or amyloid PET) if a biological diagnosis would change management, such as eligibility for anti-amyloid treatment or diagnostic uncertainty; one conclusive test is sufficient [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].
Refer to occupational therapy and low-vision services for visuospatial compensation (dressing, reading aids, home navigation and lighting) [PCA_consensus_2017].

Address safety: she must not drive, should not walk out alone until a plan is in place after three episodes of getting lost (identification, phone location sharing), and needs supervision of medicines and finances
Keep blood pressure at target and check lipids and HbA1c, given Fazekas grade 2 small vessel disease
Offer genetic testing only with pre-test and post-test genetic counselling; the result informs the family and not the patient's diagnosis [ACMG_NSGC_2011].
Disclose the diagnosis and discuss prognosis, advance directives and a healthcare proxy with the patient and her husband

avoided_actions.rationale: Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication in this presentation
No palpitations, syncope or arrhythmia; a resting ECG answers the QT question before donepezil
MRI is available and not contraindicated; CT is less sensitive for the posterior atrophy pattern

accepted: Posterior cortical atrophy variant of early-onset Alzheimer's disease

differential.key_features: Ideomotor apraxia and right-hand astereognosis overlap with CBS, but there is no rigidity, dystonia, myoclonus or alien limb, and the atrophy and hypometabolism are bilateral and parieto-occipital
Visual symptoms overlap, but there are no visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, fluctuations or REM sleep behaviour disorder

differential.diagnosis: Generalized anxiety disorder with cognitive complaints
differential.key_features: Long-standing anxiety, modestly worse, but anxiety does not produce simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, alexia or Gerstmann features, or posterior cortical atrophy
Fazekas grade 2 white matter disease may contribute, but small vessel disease does not cause a progressive posterior cortical syndrome with focal parieto-occipital atrophy
Gradual onset; excluded by MRI showing atrophy without a lesion or restricted diffusion
Visual-onset CJD progresses over weeks with myoclonus; here the course is gradual over 8 months, there is no myoclonus, and MRI shows no restricted diffusion or cortical ribboning
Ophthalmologist found no retinal or optic nerve disease, acuity 20/25 and full fields; the deficits are of higher-order visual processing

key_clinical_evidence: In posterior cortical atrophy the presenting deficits are visuospatial and visuoperceptual with relatively preserved memory; patients often see an optometrist first, and Alzheimer pathology is the most common cause [PCA_consensus_2017].
Balint features (simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, oculomotor apraxia), alexia and Gerstmann features with normal acuity and fields localise to bilateral parieto-occipital cortex, not to the eye
Giving up driving, being unable to walk out alone after getting lost and needing prompting for appointments mean instrumental independence is lost: the stage is mild dementia [NIA_AA_2011]
Escitalopram and donepezil both prolong the QT interval; a baseline ECG is reasonable before a cholinesterase inhibitor is started [NICE_NG97]

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Normal acuity, fundi and fields with simultanagnosia, optic ataxia and alexia point to higher-order visual cortex, not the eye
red_herrings.data_point: Referral from ophthalmology for reading difficulty, with an updated spectacle prescription
red_herrings.intended_effect: Pursue an ocular explanation for the reading and visual complaints

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Late-onset dementia in two relatives is consistent with sporadic Alzheimer disease, and the sister's symptoms are non-specific; genetic testing is optional and follows counselling
red_herrings.data_point: Mother with dementia at 78, maternal aunt with memory loss from her late 60s, and a sister of 55 recently assessed for irritability and anxiety
red_herrings.intended_effect: Assume an autosomal dominant or frontotemporal genetic disorder and make genetic testing the diagnostic step

sequence_constraints.reason: Obtain structural imaging before lumbar puncture to exclude a mass lesion or hydrocephalus
Amyloid biomarkers are interpreted against an established clinical syndrome; they are not a screening test.
Genetic testing follows the clinical diagnosis and pre-test counselling.

clinical_assessment.impression: MMSE 24/30 and clock drawing 2/5, with Balint features (simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, oculomotor apraxia), alexia, Gerstmann features, ideomotor apraxia and cortical sensory loss. Delayed recall 0/3 free and 2/3 with category cues. Her husband reports decline over 8 months in reading, face recognition, navigation and dressing, with conversational memory preserved. She has stopped driving, cannot walk out alone, and needs prompting for appointments, so instrumental independence is lost and the syndrome is at the mild dementia level.

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Lin Wei is a 62-year-old right-handed retired art teacher referred to the neurology outpatient clinic by her ophthalmologist for evaluation of progressive visual and cognitive complaints over approximately eight months. The patient initially presented to her optometrist six months ago complaining of increasing difficulty reading despite adequate corrected visual acuity. She described being unable to follow lines of text, frequently losing her place, and finding that words appeared to 'jump around' on the page. Her optometrist updated her prescription without significant improvement and referred her to an ophthalmologist, who found no retinal or optic nerve pathology and documented normal visual acuity and full visual fields on confrontation testing. Around the same time, her husband noticed that she was having increasing difficulty parking the car, frequently misjudging distances and bumping into curbs. She subsequently stopped driving after a minor fender bender in a parking lot three months ago. Over the past four months, the patient has developed progressive difficulty recognizing the faces of casual acquaintances, though she continues to recognize close family members by voice and context. She has become lost on three occasions while walking in her own neighborhood of twenty years, once requiring a neighbor to guide her home. She reports increasing difficulty dressing herself, specifically with buttoning shirts and orienting garments correctly, and has begun wearing pullover tops exclusively. Her husband reports that she recently could not find items on a cluttered table even when they were directly in front of her, describing that she seems to see individual objects but cannot take in the whole visual scene. Notably, the patient's conversational memory appears relatively preserved: she can recount recent family events, remembers appointments with prompting, and follows conversations without difficulty. Her husband reports that she does not repeat questions or forget recent conversations, which he finds puzzling given the severity of her other symptoms. There has been no sudden onset of any symptoms, no headache, no seizure activity, and no psychiatric symptoms beyond her longstanding anxiety, which her husband feels may have worsened modestly over the past several months. She has experienced no hallucinations, no changes in personality, and no motor symptoms. Her sleep pattern has been normal without REM sleep behavior disorder. There have been no recent infections, no weight loss, and no systemic symptoms. Her anxiety has increased somewhat in the context of these difficulties, but her mood has remained stable. The family history is notable for dementia in her mother and a maternal aunt, and her younger sister was recently evaluated for new-onset irritability and anxiety.

neurological_exam.additional: Balint syndrome features present: simultanagnosia (cannot perceive more than one object at a time in a complex visual scene), optic ataxia (misreaching under visual guidance), and oculomotor apraxia (difficulty voluntarily directing gaze to peripheral targets). Gerstmann syndrome features partially present: finger agnosia (unable to identify individual fingers when touched with eyes closed), difficulty with left-right discrimination. Alexia present: patient cannot read more than individual letters despite preserved visual acuity. Ideomotor apraxia elicited when asked to pantomime brushing teeth and using scissors. No features of parkinsonism, myoclonus, or rapid cognitive fluctuation.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact bilaterally. Heel-to-shin testing intact. Rapid alternating movements normal. However, patient demonstrates significant difficulty with visually guided reaching — overshooting when asked to touch examiner's finger with eyes open (optic ataxia), and difficulty with smooth visual pursuit when tracking a moving object across midline.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, 3 mm, reactive to light and accommodation. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Visual acuity 20/25 bilaterally (corrected). Confrontation visual fields full to finger counting in all quadrants bilaterally, but simultanagnosia elicited on bilateral simultaneous stimulation with visual extinction on the right. Facial sensation intact to light touch and pinprick. Facial movements symmetric. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius full strength. Tongue midline.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady gait with normal stride length and arm swing. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative. However, patient hesitates at doorways and nearly collides with furniture when navigating an unfamiliar examination room.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, year and month, but unsure of the exact date. Cooperative and pleasant. Affect is mildly anxious. Speech is fluent with normal rate, rhythm, and prosody. No paraphasic errors. MMSE 24/30: lost 1 point on orientation to time (date), 0/3 on delayed recall, 1 point on reading the written command (alexia), 1 point on copying intersecting pentagons; serial sevens correct. Clock drawing test scored 2/5: numbers placed outside the circle, hands not pointing to correct time. Notably, the patient was unable to describe the spatial arrangement of objects on the desk and had difficulty identifying overlapping figures (Poppelreuter test).
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk and tone normal throughout. Strength 5/5 in all muscle groups of bilateral upper and lower extremities. No pronator drift. No adventitious movements or myoclonus.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+, triceps 2+, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally. Patellar 2+, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No frontal release signs.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact throughout. Proprioception intact at bilateral great toes. Impaired graphesthesia in bilateral hands (unable to identify numbers drawn on palms). Astereognosis in right hand (unable to identify key or coin by touch alone).
